questions.title: Track one changed place
questions.question: x=4 and y=7. Replace x with 9. What is the new state?
questions.explanation: Replacement changes x to 9. Nothing in the operation writes y, so y remains 7.

questions.title: Copy, then change the original
questions.question: After x=4; y=x; x=x+3;, what is y?
questions.explanation: y received a copy of the value 4. The final assignment only writes x.

questions.title: Bits versus bytes
questions.question: How many bits are in an eight-byte value?
questions.explanation: Multiply eight bytes by eight bits per byte: 64 bits.

questions.title: Read a bit pattern
questions.question: What unsigned number is 0b1101?
questions.explanation: The set positions contribute 8+4+1=13.

questions.title: Read a hexadecimal value
questions.question: What is 0x2A in decimal?
questions.explanation: 2×16+A, with A=10, gives 42.

questions.title: One pattern, two interpretations
questions.question: An eight-bit pattern is 0xFE. Its unsigned value is 254. What is its signed two’s-complement value?
questions.explanation: The top bit is set, so subtract 256: 254−256=−2. Width is essential to this calculation.

questions.title: Your first instruction
questions.cCode:
// Put the constant 12 in RAX.
// This is a snippet: stop at the end.
questions.hint: Write the immediate first and the register destination second.
questions.explanation: movq selects 64 bits, $12 is the immediate, and %rax is the destination.

questions.title: Copy the supplied input
questions.cCode: // RDI contains x. Copy x into RAX; keep RDI unchanged.
questions.hint: Use the register as the source, not a constant.
questions.explanation: A register-to-register MOV copies all 64 bits, including values larger than 32 bits.

questions.title: Apply the rule to a different family
questions.question: R8 contains all 64 one bits. After movl $3,%r8d, what is R8?
questions.explanation: R8D is the 32-bit view of R8. Its write clears the upper 32 bits, just as writing EAX does for RAX.

questions.title: Add to a copy
questions.cCode: // RDI=x. Put x+3 in RAX and preserve RDI.
questions.explanation: MOV initializes RAX from x; ADD reads that old RAX and adds the constant.

questions.title: Keep subtraction order
questions.cCode: // RDI=x; RSI=y. Put x-y in RAX.
questions.hint: Write destination = destination - source on paper.
questions.explanation: Initializing with x makes the subtraction compute x−y rather than y−x.

questions.title: Multiply two supplied inputs
questions.cCode: // RDI=x; RSI=y. Put x*y in RAX.
questions.hint: Copy one factor to the result, then multiply by the other.
questions.explanation: The two-operand IMUL reads the old destination as a factor.

questions.title: Keep only the destination width
questions.question: What eight-bit unsigned result remains after 255+2?
questions.explanation: 257 modulo 256 is 1. The bit beyond the eight-bit width cannot stay in that destination.

questions.title: Read inputs and result
questions.question: In long difference(long x,long y) { return x-y; }, what does difference(9,4) produce?
questions.explanation: The arguments initialize x=9 and y=4. The returned expression is 9−4=5.

questions.title: Place the result where the caller expects it
questions.question: A function returns a long. In which register should its result be placed?
questions.explanation: The integer result register for this convention is RAX. RDI supplies the first argument; RSP has a separate stack role.

questions.title: Write your first complete translation
questions.cCode: long plus(long x,long y) { return x+y; }
questions.hint: Compute the sum in RAX, then return control.
questions.explanation: RDI/RSI provide the arguments. MOV and ADD produce the result in RAX; RET finishes the function.

questions.title: Read the next stored byte
questions.question: The four-byte value 0x12345678 begins at 0x100 on x86. What byte is at 0x101?
questions.explanation: Increasing addresses contain 78,56,34,12 in hexadecimal. The second byte, at 0x101, is 0x56.

questions.title: A pointer and its pointee
questions.question: p contains 0x100, and the long at 0x100 is 23. What does *p evaluate to?
questions.explanation: Dereferencing accesses the value at the address held in p. The address is 0x100; the value there is 23.

questions.title: Index versus byte offset
questions.question: A long array starts at 0x1000. What is the address of a[3]?
questions.explanation: Index 3 means 3×8=24 bytes from the base. Decimal 24 is 0x18, so the address is 0x1018.

questions.title: Setting an already-set bit
questions.question: What is 8 | 8?
questions.explanation: OR sets positions; it does not add their numeric weights twice. Bit 3 remains set and the result stays 8.

questions.title: Follow a logical shift
questions.question: As an eight-bit illustration, what is 10000000 shifted logically right by one?
questions.explanation: Each bit moves one place toward the right. SHR fills the newly open high position with zero.

questions.title: Compare without overwriting
questions.question: RDI=6 and RSI=4. After cmpq %rsi,%rdi, which is true?
options: RDI and RSI are unchanged; flags describe 6−4
questions.explanation: CMP computes destination minus source only to set flags. It does not store the numeric difference.

questions.title: Translate a zero test
questions.hint: Default the result to false, and skip the true assignment when equal.
solutions:
movq $0,%rax
cmpq $0,%rdi
je done
movq $1,%rax
done: ret
questions.explanation: JE uses the equality flag; negative values are nonzero too.

questions.title: Restore saved values
questions.question: You push RAX and then RCX to preserve them. Which restore order recovers both originals?
questions.explanation: The most recently pushed value is on top, so restore RCX before RAX.

questions.title: Distinguish register mode from memory mode
questions.question: Given that 48 89 c3 encodes movq %rax,%rbx and 48 89 03 encodes movq %rax,(%rbx), what changes?
options: Only the numeric value being copied
Whether the destination is RBX itself or memory at RBX
The copy changes from 64 bits to 8 bits
questions.explanation: The destination mode changes. Both forms copy 64-bit data, but one writes a register and one writes an addressed memory location.

questions.title: Read the C expression before narrowing
questions.question: In this model, unsigned char x=0x87 promotes to a 32-bit int. What is the value of x<<2 before storing it back into a byte?
questions.explanation: The unsigned-char value 135 promotes to int, and 135×4=540 fits in int. Assigning 540 to an unsigned char afterward would yield 28, but that is a separate narrowing step.
